topics.title: The Stone Age and Bronze Age
topics.intro: The Stone Age lasted for hundreds of thousands of years. People went from hunting mammoths with flint spears to farming, building villages like Skara Brae and raising Stonehenge. Then they learned to make bronze.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between the Old Stone Age and the New Stone Age.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} would miss most if {she} lived in the Stone Age.

visual.caption: All the dates are “about”. The Old Stone Age began hundreds of thousands of years before this line starts, and the Iron Age lasted until the Romans came in AD 43.

topics.title: The Iron Age and the Celts
topics.intro: From about 800 BC, people in Britain learned to make iron. Iron ore was much easier to find than the copper and tin needed for bronze, so more people could have strong tools. Iron Age tribes built hill forts, drove chariots and followed priests called druids.
topics.teach: Explain why a hill fort was a good place to defend.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to design an Iron Age hill fort with ditches and a gate.

topics.title: Inside the Roman army
topics.intro: The Roman army was one of the best-trained armies in history. Soldiers called legionaries trained every day, marched in step and fought as a team.
topics.teach: Explain what a legionary carried and what each thing was for.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which would be harder: marching 20 miles in armour, or building a fort at the end of it.

topics.title: Boudica, the warrior queen
topics.intro: In about AD 60 or 61, Boudica, queen of the Iceni tribe, led a huge rebellion against the Romans. Her army destroyed three Roman towns before the Romans finally defeated her.
topics.teach: Explain why Boudica rebelled against the Romans.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether {she} thinks Boudica was a hero, and why.

steps: The Romans take the Iceni lands
Colchester, London and St Albans destroyed
A smaller Roman army defeats her
visual.caption: Boudica’s revolt, AD 60 or 61.

topics.title: Roman life and what the Romans left us
topics.intro: The Romans ruled Britain for nearly 400 years. They built towns, villas, baths and straight roads, and left behind words, numbers and even letters written on wood.
topics.teach: Explain three things the Romans left behind that we still use.
topics.talk: Look for a Roman road, a Roman numeral or a Latin word together this week.

visual.caption: The Romans ruled Britain for nearly 400 years.

topics.title: Anglo-Saxons and Scots
topics.intro: After the Romans left, Angles, Saxons and Jutes sailed over from northern Europe and set up kingdoms. In the north, the Scots and Picts lived. England gets its name from the Angles!
topics.teach: Explain what was found at Sutton Hoo and why it matters.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which day of the week is named after an Anglo-Saxon god.

visual.caption: Some of these dates are “about”: 450 and 624.

topics.title: Vikings and Anglo-Saxons: the struggle for England
topics.intro: For about 250 years, Vikings and Anglo-Saxons raided, fought, made peace and traded. In the end, England became one kingdom.
topics.teach: Explain how Alfred the Great defended Wessex from the Vikings.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to write {her} name in Viking runes (find a rune alphabet in a library book).

topics.title: Ancient Greece
topics.intro: About 2,500 years ago, the cities of Ancient Greece gave the world the Olympic Games, democracy, theatre and many great thinkers. Athens and Sparta were very different cities.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between Athens and Sparta.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which Greek god or goddess {she} would like to be, and why.

topics.title: The first great civilisations
topics.intro: More than 4,000 years ago, the first great civilisations grew up beside rivers: in Sumer, in the Indus Valley and in Egypt. They built cities and invented writing.
topics.teach: Explain why the first cities were built beside rivers.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} would need to build a city from nothing.

visual.caption: All the dates are “about”. When the first cities grew, Britain was still in the Stone Age.

topics.title: Castles under attack
topics.intro: Attacking a castle was very hard. Attackers used giant catapults, siege towers, battering rams and tunnels, and defenders kept making castles stronger.
topics.teach: Explain why a concentric castle was so hard to attack.
topics.talk: Build a castle from cushions or blocks and ask {him} how {she} would defend it.

topics.title: The Battle of Britain
topics.intro: In the summer of 1940, the German air force tried to defeat Britain’s Royal Air Force. Radar, brave pilots from many countries and a clever control system helped Britain hold on.
topics.teach: Explain how radar helped the RAF.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why Churchill called the pilots “the Few”.

steps: Radar spots planes over the sea
The Observer Corps track them over land
WAAF plotters mark them on a map
Fighters are sent up to meet them
visual.caption: Fighter Command’s warning and control system, 1940.

topics.title: The Home Front
topics.intro: During the Second World War, ordinary people helped too: they kept the blackout, grew vegetables, worked on farms and in factories, and sheltered from air raids.
topics.teach: Explain how families kept safe during an air raid.
topics.talk: Ask an older relative if their family had an Anderson shelter or grew vegetables for victory.

topics.title: Thinking like a historian
topics.intro: Historians use dates, put events in order, and look at evidence from the past. Some evidence was made at the time; some was made much later.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a primary source and a secondary source.
topics.talk: Find something old at home (a photo, a coin) and ask {him} what it tells you about the past.

visual.caption: BC years count down to 1 BC; then AD years count up from AD 1. There is no year 0.

topics.title: The Normans in charge
topics.intro: After 1066, William the Conqueror and the Normans took control of England. They built castles everywhere, counted everything in the Domesday Book, and set up the feudal system.
topics.teach: Explain how the feudal system worked, from the king down to the peasants.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what the Domesday Book might have said about your town.

c.note: given land by a baron; fight for him

visual.caption: The feudal system, from most powerful to least.

topics.title: Shang China
topics.intro: About 3,600 years ago, the Shang dynasty ruled part of China beside the Yellow River. They made beautiful bronze and wrote questions to their ancestors on bones.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what question {she} would write on an oracle bone.

visual.caption: All the dates are “about”. The Shang ruled China while Britain was in the Bronze Age.

items.prompt: Put the three parts of the Stone Age in order, earliest first.
items.explain: Palaeo means old, meso means middle and neo means new. “Lithic” means stone.

visual.caption: Palaeo = old, meso = middle, neo = new; lithic = stone.

items.prompt: What big change happened in the Neolithic (New Stone Age)?

options.text: People began farming and living in villages
People began driving carts with engines
options.feedback: Engines came thousands of years later.
Iron came much later, in the Iron Age.

items.explain: Farming reached Britain about 6,000 years ago. People settled down to grow crops and keep animals.

items.prompt: Early Stone Age people moved around to hunt animals and collect plants. What are they called?
items.explain: They hunted animals and gathered berries, nuts and roots.

items.prompt: Which Stone Age village in Orkney was uncovered by a great storm in 1850?
items.explain: A storm blew the sand away and revealed stone houses about 5,000 years old, with stone beds and dressers.

items.prompt: Some of the smaller stones at Stonehenge, the bluestones, came from far away. Where from?
items.explain: They were moved about 150 miles, probably by people pulling them on sledges and rollers.

items.prompt: Cheddar Man is Britain’s oldest almost complete skeleton. About how long ago did he live?
items.explain: He was found in Gough’s Cave in Cheddar Gorge, Somerset, in 1903. He lived in the Middle Stone Age.

items.prompt: A rich grave found near Stonehenge in 2002 belonged to a man buried about 4,300 years ago with arrowheads, copper knives and gold. What do we call him?
items.explain: Tests on his teeth show he grew up in the Alps area of central Europe, so he had travelled a very long way.

items.prompt: Bronze is made by mixing which two metals?

options.feedback: Gold and silver were used for jewellery. Bronze is copper and tin.
Steel is made from iron. Bronze is copper and tin.

items.explain: Tin was mined in Cornwall. Bronze tools and weapons were harder than copper ones.

items.prompt: At Grime’s Graves in Norfolk, Stone Age people dug deep mines to find which stone for tools?
items.explain: Flint can be chipped into a very sharp edge for axes and arrowheads.

items.prompt: Stone Age people did not write. How do we know about them?

options.text: From the things they left behind

options.feedback: There was no writing in Stone Age Britain.
Photographs were first taken about 200 years ago.

items.explain: Archaeologists study objects and remains to work out how people lived.

items.prompt: About when did the Iron Age begin in Britain?
items.explain: It lasted until the Romans arrived in AD 43.

items.prompt: Why was iron better than bronze for tools and weapons?

options.text: Iron ore was easy to find and made strong tools

options.feedback: Bronze is actually shinier. Iron ore was easier to find, and iron tools could be made very strong.
Iron does rust!

items.explain: Iron ore was found in lots of places, so more people could have strong tools.

items.prompt: Which huge Iron Age hill fort in Dorset has enormous banks and ditches?
items.explain: It is one of the largest hill forts in Europe. It was not a castle with stone walls, but earth banks.

items.prompt: Why did Iron Age people build forts on hilltops?

options.text: It was warmer at the top
options.feedback: Hills are usually colder and windier!

options.text: There was more water up high
options.feedback: Water was usually easier to find lower down.

items.explain: Ditches and banks around the top made attackers climb uphill.

items.prompt: What were Celtic priests and wise people called?
items.explain: Druids led ceremonies and were also judges and teachers.

items.prompt: Iron Age warriors rode into battle on a light, two-wheeled cart pulled by ponies. What was it called?
items.explain: Julius Caesar wrote about how skilfully British warriors drove their chariots.

items.prompt: What was a torc?
items.explain: The Great Torc from Snettisham in Norfolk is made of gold and is in the British Museum.

items.prompt: What did some Iron Age tribes make for the first time in Britain, near the end of the Iron Age?

options.feedback: Books came much later.
Bicycles were invented in the 1800s.

items.explain: Some coins show the names of tribal leaders, which helps historians.

items.prompt: Where was the fire in an Iron Age roundhouse?
items.explain: The smoke drifted up through the thatched roof. Families cooked, ate and slept around it.

items.prompt: Iron Age Britain was not one country. How was it organised?

options.text: Ruled by one king in London
options.feedback: There was no London yet! The Romans founded it.

options.text: Ruled by the Romans from Rome
options.feedback: The Romans came at the END of the Iron Age.

items.explain: Tribes included the Iceni, the Brigantes and the Catuvellauni.

items.prompt: Which famous Roman general visited Britain with his army in 55 and 54 BC, but did not stay?
items.explain: Caesar won some battles but went back to Gaul (France). The real invasion came almost 100 years later.

items.prompt: Which Roman emperor sent the army that invaded Britain in AD 43?
items.explain: Claudius even came to Britain himself, and is said to have brought elephants!

items.prompt: What was an ordinary Roman foot soldier called?
items.explain: Legionaries had to be Roman citizens and served for about 25 years.

items.prompt: Who commanded a group of about 80 legionaries?
items.explain: The name comes from the Latin for a hundred, though a century usually had 80 men.

items.prompt: Which of these did a legionary NOT carry?

options.feedback: The gladius was his main weapon.
The scutum protected him and his friends.
He threw his pilum before the armies met.

items.explain: Longbows were used by English archers more than a thousand years later.

items.prompt: In the “testudo” (tortoise) formation, how did soldiers use their shields?

options.text: They locked them into a shell
They threw them at the enemy
options.feedback: Shields were for protection.

options.text: They used them as little boats
options.feedback: Not in battle!

items.explain: The shell of shields protected them from arrows and stones as they moved forward.

items.prompt: At the end of a long day’s march, what did Roman soldiers build?

options.text: A camp with a ditch and a fence
A tall castle made of stone
options.feedback: Stone castles came much later. They built a quick camp every night.
They always protected their camp.

items.explain: Every soldier carried tools for digging, so they could build a safe camp in a few hours.

items.prompt: Which British leader fought the Romans for years, was captured, and was spared by Emperor Claudius after a brave speech in Rome?
items.explain: He was handed over to the Romans in AD 51. Claudius was so impressed by his speech that he let him live.

items.prompt: Soldiers in the Roman army who were not Roman citizens were called…
items.explain: Auxiliaries came from all over the empire. After 25 years they could become citizens.

items.prompt: Roman soldiers wore tough leather sandals with iron nails in the soles. What were they called?
items.explain: The nails gave grip, a bit like football boots.

items.prompt: Boudica was queen of which tribe?
items.explain: The Iceni lived in what is now Norfolk and Suffolk.

items.prompt: Why did Boudica rebel?

options.text: The Romans took her tribe’s land
She wanted to become a Roman
options.feedback: She was fighting AGAINST Roman rule.

options.text: The Romans stole her best chariot
options.feedback: It was much more serious: they took the tribe’s lands and treated her family cruelly.

items.explain: Her husband, King Prasutagus, had wanted to share his kingdom with the emperor. Instead, the Romans took everything.

items.prompt: Which three Roman towns did Boudica’s army destroy?

options.feedback: Those were Roman towns, but not the ones Boudica attacked.
She fought in Britain.

items.explain: In Roman times they were called Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium.

items.prompt: About when was Boudica’s revolt?
items.explain: Historians are not sure which of the two years it was.

items.prompt: How did the revolt end?

options.text: A smaller Roman army beat her

options.feedback: She was defeated.

options.text: The Romans left Britain for ever
options.feedback: They stayed for another 350 years.

items.explain: The Roman governor, Suetonius Paulinus, chose a narrow battlefield where the Romans’ training mattered most.

items.prompt: Most of what we know about Boudica comes from Roman writers like Tacitus. Why should we be careful with their stories?

options.text: They were on the Roman side
Romans did not know how to write
options.feedback: Romans wrote a lot! The problem is whose side they were on.
They wrote in Latin.

items.explain: The Iceni left no written records, so we only hear the Roman side.

items.prompt: A famous statue of Boudica stands near the Houses of Parliament in London. What is she riding?
items.explain: The bronze statue was put up in 1902.

items.prompt: Where was the Roman governor when Boudica’s revolt began?
items.explain: He was attacking the druids on Anglesey. He hurried back with his army, but could not save London.

items.prompt: In about AD 122, which emperor ordered a great wall to be built across the north of England?
items.explain: Hadrian’s Wall ran about 73 miles from coast to coast.

items.prompt: What are the Vindolanda tablets, found near Hadrian’s Wall?

options.feedback: They are writing tablets, not medicine.

options.text: Stone tablets with laws on them
options.feedback: They are thin slices of wood with ink writing.

items.explain: One is a birthday party invitation from a lady called Claudia Severa. Another mentions socks and underpants sent to a soldier!

items.prompt: What was a hypocaust?
items.explain: Hot air from a fire flowed under the floor, which rested on little pillars of tiles.

items.prompt: Which English city is named after the Roman baths built around its hot springs?
items.explain: The Romans called it Aquae Sulis. You can still see the Great Bath today.

items.prompt: Which huge Roman palace in West Sussex has amazing mosaic floors?
items.explain: A mosaic is a picture made from thousands of tiny coloured tiles.

items.prompt: Why did the Romans build long, straight roads?

options.text: So soldiers and supplies could travel quickly
Because they did not know how to make bends
options.feedback: They could make bends, but straight was quickest.
Races were held on special racetracks called circuses.

items.explain: A straight road is the shortest route. Watling Street and the Fosse Way are famous Roman roads.

items.prompt: Which month is named after Julius Caesar?

options.feedback: June is named after the goddess Juno.
January is named after the god Janus.

items.explain: And August is named after the Emperor Augustus.

items.prompt: Which great city was founded by the Romans and called Londinium?
items.explain: The Romans built a bridge over the Thames, and a town grew up beside it.

items.prompt: About when did the Roman army leave Britain?
items.explain: Rome itself was under attack, so the soldiers were needed at home.

items.prompt: Which of these do we still use from the Romans?

options.text: Roman numerals and many words from Latin

options.feedback: We don’t ride chariots today!
We use pounds and pence now.

items.explain: Words like “aquarium” (aqua = water) and “century” (centum = a hundred) come from Latin.

items.prompt: Where did the Angles, Saxons and Jutes come from?

options.text: Italy, near the city of Rome
options.feedback: That is where the Romans came from.
Nobody in Europe knew about America then.

items.explain: They began to arrive from about AD 450, after the Romans left.

items.prompt: The word “England” comes from “Angle-land”. Which people is it named after?
items.explain: Angle-land became England.

items.prompt: Which of these was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom?

options.feedback: That is a made-up place from an old legend!
Rome was in Italy.

items.explain: The big kingdoms included Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria, East Anglia and Kent.

items.prompt: In 1939, a buried ship full of treasure, including a famous helmet, was found in Suffolk. Where?
items.explain: It was probably the grave of King Rædwald of East Anglia, who died about AD 624. The helmet is in the British Museum.

items.prompt: In AD 597, a monk was sent from Rome to Kent to spread Christianity. Who was he?
items.explain: He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.

items.prompt: Which Anglo-Saxon monk at Jarrow wrote a famous history of the English people?
items.explain: Bede finished his history in AD 731. He helped make AD dates popular.

items.prompt: Which king of Mercia built a giant earth bank along the border with Wales?
items.explain: Offa’s Dyke is still there, and you can walk along it.

items.prompt: Which day of the week is named after the Anglo-Saxon god Woden?

options.feedback: Thursday is named after Thunor (Thor), the thunder god.
Friday is named after the goddess Frigg.

items.explain: Woden’s day became Wednesday. That is why there is a silent d in it!

items.prompt: What were most Anglo-Saxon houses made of?

options.feedback: Most Anglo-Saxons built with wood.
That is modern!

items.explain: The most important building in a village was the lord’s great hall, where feasts were held.

items.prompt: In early Scotland, which two peoples were later joined together under one king?

options.feedback: They were never in Scotland together like that.
The Iceni lived in the east of England.

items.explain: The Scots came over from Ireland; the Picts lived in the north and east. They were united in about AD 843.

items.prompt: In AD 793, Vikings attacked a famous monastery on a holy island off the coast of Northumberland. What was it called?
items.explain: This raid shocked everyone and is often seen as the start of the Viking Age in Britain.

items.prompt: In 878, Alfred the Great defeated the Viking leader Guthrum at which battle?
items.explain: Afterwards Guthrum agreed to become a Christian, and England was divided between them.

items.prompt: What was the Danelaw?

options.text: The part of England ruled by Vikings

options.feedback: Ha! It was land ruled by the Danes (Vikings).
It was an area of land.

items.explain: After Edington, the north and east of England became the Danelaw. Alfred kept Wessex.

items.prompt: How did Alfred protect Wessex from more Viking attacks?

options.text: He built walled towns called burhs

options.feedback: He stayed and defended Wessex.

options.text: He gave the Vikings all his gold each year
options.feedback: He built defences instead.

items.explain: If the Vikings attacked, people could reach a burh quickly. Many burhs became towns we know today.

items.prompt: There is a famous legend about Alfred hiding from the Vikings. What did he do?

options.text: He dressed up as a Viking
options.feedback: That is not the famous legend.
No whales in this story!

items.explain: It is a legend, so we cannot be sure it happened, but it shows how hard times were for Alfred.

items.prompt: Who became the first king of all England, in 927?
items.explain: Athelstan was Alfred’s grandson.

items.prompt: The Vikings called the city of York…
items.explain: Jorvik was a busy trading town. Archaeologists found Viking houses, shoes and even poo there!

items.prompt: What were the letters of the Viking alphabet called?
items.explain: Runes were made of straight lines, which are easy to carve into wood and stone.

items.prompt: Which Viking god carried a mighty hammer?

options.feedback: Odin was the chief god, with one eye and two ravens.
Loki was the trickster god.

items.explain: Viking warriors hoped to go to Valhalla, Odin’s great hall, when they died.

items.prompt: Which Viking king ruled England from 1016, and also Denmark and Norway?
items.explain: A famous story says he sat on the beach and showed that even a king cannot stop the tide.

items.prompt: In which year did the first recorded Olympic Games take place, in Olympia?
items.explain: The games honoured Zeus. Only men could compete, and winners got a crown of olive leaves.

items.prompt: Athens is famous for inventing democracy. What does democracy mean?

options.text: Rule by one king or queen
options.feedback: That is a monarchy.
Democracy means the people decide.

items.explain: In Athens only free men could vote, but the idea spread across the world.

items.prompt: What was Sparta famous for?

options.feedback: Athens was more famous for theatre.
Pyramids were in Egypt.

items.explain: Spartan soldiers were some of the best-trained in Greece.

items.prompt: In the legend of Troy, how did the Greeks get inside the city?

options.text: They hid inside a wooden horse
They dug a tunnel under the walls
options.feedback: The trick was a wooden horse.
No flying in this legend!

items.explain: The Trojans pulled the horse inside as a prize. At night, the soldiers climbed out.

items.prompt: The marathon race is named after a battle in 490 BC. Who won the Battle of Marathon?
items.explain: A legend says a messenger ran all the way to Athens with the news. Today’s marathon is 26.2 miles.

items.prompt: Who was the king of the Greek gods?
items.explain: Zeus ruled from Mount Olympus and threw thunderbolts. (Jupiter was his Roman name.)

items.prompt: The city of Athens was named after which goddess of wisdom?
items.explain: Her great temple, the Parthenon, still stands on a hill called the Acropolis.

items.prompt: The word “alphabet” comes from the first two Greek letters. What are they?

options.feedback: Close, but in Greek they are called alpha and beta.
Omega is the LAST Greek letter.

items.explain: Alpha + beta = alphabet.

items.prompt: Greek foot soldiers, called hoplites, fought in a tight block with overlapping shields. What was it called?

options.feedback: The testudo was the Roman tortoise.
That was a Viking ship.

items.explain: Each soldier’s shield also helped protect the man beside him, so they had to stick together.

items.prompt: What did the ancient Greeks give us that we still enjoy today?

options.feedback: Television was invented in 1926.
Modern football came from England much later.

items.explain: Greek actors wore masks and performed in huge open-air theatres.

items.prompt: Why were the first cities built beside rivers?

options.text: People liked the noise of rivers
options.feedback: It was about water, food and transport.
The Romans came much later.

items.explain: Rivers flooded and left rich mud. Farmers grew extra food, so cities could grow.

items.prompt: About 5,200 years ago, people in Sumer invented one of the first kinds of writing, pressed into clay with a reed. What is it called?
items.explain: Cuneiform means wedge-shaped, because of the shapes the reed made.

items.prompt: Sumer was in Mesopotamia, which means “the land between the rivers”. Which modern country is it in?
items.explain: The two rivers are the Tigris and the Euphrates.

items.prompt: Which very important invention were the Sumerians among the first to use, about 5,500 years ago?

options.feedback: That was 1876!
That was 1903.

items.explain: First for making pots, then for carts.

items.prompt: Which ancient civilisation built the cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, with neat streets and drains?
items.explain: They lived about 4,500 years ago in what is now Pakistan and north-west India.

items.prompt: What was amazing about Indus Valley cities?

options.text: They had planned streets and drains
They were built on the Moon
options.feedback: They were beside the River Indus.
Electricity came thousands of years later.

items.explain: Many houses had their own bathroom, connected to drains under the streets.

items.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
items.explain: About 3200 BC, about 2560 BC, 776 BC, AD 43.

items.prompt: Once farmers grew more food than they needed, what could other people do?

options.text: Do other jobs, like making pots

options.feedback: Everyone still needs food!
Extra food let cities grow.

items.explain: Spare food meant some people could become potters, builders, priests and scribes.

items.prompt: The Sumerians built huge stepped temples. What were they called?
items.explain: A ziggurat looks like a pyramid made of giant steps, with a temple at the top.

items.prompt: Which giant siege machine used a heavy counterweight to fling huge stones at castle walls?
items.explain: King Edward I had an enormous trebuchet called the “Warwolf” built to attack Stirling Castle in 1304.

items.prompt: What did attackers push up to the castle walls so soldiers could climb across the top?
items.explain: Siege towers were tall wooden towers on wheels, often covered in wet animal skins so they would not burn.

items.prompt: What was used to smash down a castle gate?
items.explain: Soldiers swung a huge tree trunk, often under a roof to protect them.

items.prompt: In 1215, how did King John’s army bring down a tower of Rochester Castle?

options.text: They dug a tunnel under it
They flew over it in a balloon
options.feedback: Balloons came hundreds of years later.
It was a siege!

items.explain: When the props burned away, the tunnel collapsed and the tower fell in.

items.prompt: What is a concentric castle?

options.text: A castle with rings of walls

options.feedback: Concentric means circles with the same centre.

options.text: A castle with no walls at all
options.feedback: It has MORE walls, not fewer.

items.explain: If attackers got over the outer wall, they were trapped between two walls. Beaumaris in Wales is a famous example.

items.prompt: Which king built a ring of mighty castles in Wales, such as Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech and Beaumaris?
items.explain: He built them after conquering Wales in the 1280s.

items.prompt: If attackers could not break in, what else could they do?

options.text: Give up and go home at once
options.feedback: Sometimes they did, but often they waited.
Castles did not have doorbells!

items.explain: A siege could last for months. Castles had wells and food stores to hold out.

items.prompt: Defenders could drop stones through holes in the ceiling of the gateway. What were these holes called?
items.explain: Attackers who got through the gate were still not safe.

items.prompt: Narrow openings in castle walls let archers shoot out but were hard to hit from outside. What were they called?
items.explain: They were wide on the inside and very narrow on the outside.

items.prompt: In which year was the Battle of Britain fought?
items.explain: It lasted from July to October 1940.

items.prompt: What was the Battle of Britain?

options.feedback: It was fought in the air.
It was in 1940, with aeroplanes.

items.explain: Germany wanted to control the skies before trying to invade. The RAF stopped them.

items.prompt: How did radar help the RAF?

options.text: It spotted enemy planes far away

options.feedback: Radar finds planes; it does not hide them.
Radar is for seeing far away.

items.explain: A chain of radar stations along the coast, called Chain Home, sent out radio waves that bounced back off planes.

items.prompt: Radar could not see planes once they had crossed the coast. Who tracked them over land, with binoculars?
items.explain: Thousands of volunteers watched the skies from posts all over the country.

steps: Radar spots planes over the sea
The Observer Corps track them over land
WAAF plotters mark them on a map
Fighters are sent up to meet them

items.prompt: The Spitfire is the most famous fighter. Which other RAF fighter shot down even more enemy planes in the battle?

options.feedback: Concorde was a passenger jet, first flown in 1969.
That was the first aeroplane, in 1903.

items.explain: There were more Hurricanes than Spitfires in 1940, and they were tough and steady.

items.prompt: Winston Churchill said, “Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.” Who were “the Few”?

options.feedback: He meant the pilots.
He was thanking the RAF pilots.

items.explain: There were only about 3,000 RAF aircrew in the battle, protecting millions of people.

items.prompt: Where did the RAF pilots in the Battle of Britain come from?

options.feedback: Pilots came from all over the world.
There were a few Americans, but pilots came from many countries.

items.explain: The Polish 303 Squadron was one of the most successful of all.

items.prompt: In the operations rooms, what did members of the Women’s Auxiliary Air Force (WAAF) do?

options.text: Tracked planes on big map tables
Flew the fighter planes in battle
options.feedback: Women did not fly in combat in 1940, but some flew planes between airfields.

options.text: Cooked all the meals for pilots
options.feedback: Their job was tracking the battle.

items.explain: Commanders looked down at the table and decided which squadrons to send.

items.prompt: Who was in charge of RAF Fighter Command and built its warning and control system?
items.explain: His system joined radar, observers, map rooms and squadrons together.

items.prompt: Which day is remembered as Battle of Britain Day?
items.explain: On 15 September 1940 the RAF beat off two huge attacks. Soon afterwards the invasion plan was put off.

items.prompt: What was the Blitz?

options.feedback: It was the bombing of cities.
It was a long period of air raids.

items.explain: Blitz is short for the German word “Blitzkrieg”, meaning lightning war. London was bombed for 57 nights in a row.

items.prompt: Which air-raid shelter was half-buried in the garden and made of curved steel sheets?
items.explain: Families covered them with earth, and some grew vegetables on top!

items.prompt: Which shelter was a strong steel cage that went indoors and could be used as a table?
items.explain: Families crawled inside it during a raid.

items.prompt: Where did many Londoners shelter during air raids?

options.feedback: Roofs were the most dangerous place!
They went underground.

items.explain: Thousands of people slept on the platforms of the Tube.

items.prompt: Why did everyone have to keep a “blackout” at night?

options.text: So bombers could not see the towns

options.feedback: The main reason was to hide towns from bombers.

options.text: So children would go to sleep
options.feedback: Nice idea, but it was to hide from bombers.

items.explain: Thick curtains covered every window, and street lights were turned off. Wardens shouted, “Put that light out!”

items.prompt: Women who did farm work during the war were part of the Women’s Land Army. What were they nicknamed?
items.explain: They ploughed fields, milked cows and drove tractors, so Britain had enough food.

items.prompt: What did the “Dig for Victory” campaign ask people to do?

options.text: Dig tunnels all the way to Germany
options.feedback: It was about growing food at home.
It was about vegetables!

items.explain: Ships bringing food were being attacked, so growing your own helped everyone.

items.prompt: What did every child carry in a cardboard box, just in case?
items.explain: Luckily, gas was never used on Britain’s towns.

items.prompt: Men who were too old or young to join the army, or did vital jobs, could volunteer to defend their town. What was this group called?
items.explain: The TV comedy “Dad’s Army” is about the Home Guard.

items.prompt: Why was food rationed during the war?

options.text: So everyone got a fair share

options.feedback: It was about fair shares when food was scarce.
Shops were open, but food was limited.

items.explain: Rationing began in January 1940. Everyone had a ration book.

items.prompt: People had street parties when the war in Europe ended. What was that day called?
items.explain: VE means Victory in Europe. It was 8 May 1945.

items.prompt: Which happened earlier: 500 BC or 200 BC?

options.feedback: BC years count DOWN towards AD 1, so 500 BC is further back in time.
They are 300 years apart.

items.explain: BC years count backwards: the bigger the number, the longer ago.

visual.caption: The bigger the BC number, the longer ago.

items.prompt: What does AD stand for?

options.feedback: Ha! It is Latin: Anno Domini, “in the year of the Lord”.
It is Latin: Anno Domini.

items.explain: AD years count up from the year Christians believed Jesus was born. Some people write CE and BCE instead.

items.prompt: How many years are in a century?
items.explain: Cent means a hundred, like a centipede with (supposedly) 100 legs.

items.prompt: How many years are in a decade?
items.explain: Dec means ten.

items.prompt: Which of these is a PRIMARY source about the Romans?

options.text: A history book written last year
options.feedback: That was made long afterwards: a secondary source.
Films are made much later: secondary sources.

items.explain: A primary source comes from the time itself. A secondary source is made later by someone studying the past.

items.prompt: Which of these is a SECONDARY source about the Vikings?

options.text: A modern book about Viking life
A Viking sword found in a river
options.feedback: That object comes from the time: a primary source.
They were carved at the time: primary.

items.explain: Secondary sources are useful too, because historians bring lots of evidence together.

items.prompt: Who digs carefully in the ground to find things from the past?
items.explain: Archaeologists use trowels and brushes and record exactly where everything is found.

items.prompt: An object made by people in the past, like a coin or a pot, is called an…
items.explain: Artefacts are clues to how people lived.

items.prompt: In which century was 1066?

options.feedback: The 1000s are the 11th century, just as the 1900s were the 20th century.
The 1500s were the 16th century.

items.explain: Years 1001 to 1100 make the 11th century. For a year like 1066, the century number is one more than the number of hundreds.

items.prompt: Which year came straight after 1 BC?

options.feedback: There was no year 0! It goes 1 BC, then AD 1.
2 BC came BEFORE 1 BC.

items.explain: The calendar jumps from 1 BC to AD 1.

visual.caption: 1 BC is followed straight away by AD 1. There is no year 0.

items.prompt: In 1086, William the Conqueror sent people all over England to record who owned what land and animals. What is this record called?
items.explain: It still exists and you can look up almost any old village in it.

items.prompt: What was a motte and bailey castle?

options.text: A wooden tower on a mound

options.feedback: They were earth and wood at first.
It was a castle.

items.explain: They could be built in a few weeks. Later many were rebuilt in stone.

items.prompt: Put the feudal system in order, from most powerful to least.
items.explain: The king gave land to barons, barons gave land to knights, and peasants worked the land.

c.note: given land by a baron; fight for him

visual.caption: The feudal system, from most powerful to least.

items.prompt: Which great stone tower did William build in London?
items.explain: The White Tower is the heart of the Tower of London. It was built to show Londoners who was in charge.

items.prompt: The Normans spoke French. Which English words come from Norman French?

options.feedback: Those are older English words. Peasants raised cows and pigs; the Normans ate “boeuf” and “porc”.
Those are Old English words.

items.explain: English took thousands of words from Norman French.

items.prompt: Why did William want the Domesday Book made?

options.feedback: It is a record of land and animals.
It was about land and taxes.

items.explain: People said it was like Judgement Day (“Doomsday”): there was no escaping it!

items.prompt: Why did the Normans later rebuild many wooden castles in stone?

options.feedback: Stone was actually more work. It was about strength and fire.
Stone castles were cold! It was about strength.

items.explain: A wooden tower could be set on fire by attackers.

items.prompt: What did most peasants (villeins) have to do?

options.feedback: That was for knights.
They worked very hard.

items.explain: They could not leave the village without the lord’s permission.

items.prompt: About how long ago did the Shang dynasty begin in China?
items.explain: The Shang ruled from about 1600 BC to about 1046 BC.

items.prompt: Which river did the Shang live beside?
items.explain: Its mud is yellow, which gives the river its name.

items.prompt: What were oracle bones?

options.text: Bones used to ask the ancestors

options.feedback: They were animal bones used to ask questions.
They were used to ask the ancestors questions.

items.explain: They are the oldest Chinese writing we have, and many Chinese characters come from them.

items.prompt: What were the Shang especially skilled at making?

options.feedback: Those came about 3,000 years later.
Plastic is very modern.

items.explain: Their bronze pots were used in ceremonies for the ancestors.

items.prompt: Why are oracle bones so important to historians today?

options.text: They have the oldest Chinese writing

options.feedback: They are from people, not dinosaurs.
They were for asking questions, and now they are evidence.

items.explain: They tell us about Shang kings, battles, weather and harvests.

items.prompt: Which Shang queen was also a general who led armies? Her tomb was found in 1976.
items.explain: Her tomb was full of bronze, jade and weapons.
